items.title: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.originalTitle: Ukraine races to field faster interceptors as Russia hammers its energy grid
items.summary: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries. Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

evidenceRecords.text: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia is still using fast jet-powered drones to batter Ukraine’s energy facilities, bridges and other critical infrastructure at speeds beyond the reach of most of Kyiv’s drone interceptors, despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s unilateral announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between the two countries.
Russia began using the jets heavily in July, when their numbers jumped fivefold from the previous month.

They can now reach speeds of up to 373 mph (600 km/h) — more than three times the speed of the propeller-driven Geran-2 drones they evolved from — far exceeding the top velocity of the average Ukrainian interceptor drone, air force officials told lawmakers last week.
To stop the drones, Ukraine must instead rely on F-16s, newly installed machine gun turrets that use artificial intelligence to aim and costly air-defense missiles that are in short supply globally.
“Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refining and the energy sector in general for two days after the American president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector.

But Russia did not listen to the American president,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after jets seriously damaged a gas production facility in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday night.
Russia launched 167 missiles and drones overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, including 77 jet-powered drones, which officials said struck one of Kyiv’s main power plants and left 600,000 without power.

Ukraine’s Air Force says they are beginning to field more effective countermeasures, but with Russia continuing to optimize the design of jet-powered drones to destroy critical infrastructure, the development of jets and anti-jet interceptors has become the latest neck-and-neck technology race on the battlefield.

Iran shipped Russia its first Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 drones in mid-August 2022, and Moscow rebranded them the Geran-1 and Geran-2 and was firing them at Ukrainian civilian infrastructure by that October.

Those propeller-driven drones were slow enough for Ukraine to build an economical defense around mobile fire teams and cheap interceptor drones rather than spending scarce missiles on every Shahed, and in February the interceptors accounted for more than 70% of Shahed downings over Kyiv .

items.title: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.originalTitle: Sikorsky’s Nomad 100 VTOL Drone Is Now Quad-Packed In A Container For Rapid Deployment
items.summary: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container. The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure. The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

evidenceRecords.text: Sikorsky has unveiled a concept for a containerized deployment package for its Nomad 100 vertical takeoff and landing uncrewed aircraft system (VTOL UAS), combining four aircraft and their support equipment inside a single 20-foot shipping container.
The company is pitching the Nomad 100 Fast Pack as a way to rapidly establish autonomous air capabilities at locations without runways or other conventional support infrastructure.
The concept was unveiled on October 12 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention in Washington, D.C., where TWZ is in attendance.

It comes as the U.S. military seeks to expand its inventory of uncrewed systems and distribute capabilities across more dispersed operating locations, particularly in preparation for a potential large-scale conflict with China in the Indo-Pacific.
Rendering of the Nomad 100 Fast Pack in action.

Courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company Rendering courtesy of Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company “Military commanders are asking for capability that enables them to deploy worldwide into austere environments,” said Ramsey Bentley, director of Sikorsky Advanced Concepts, speaking at AUSA.
They want greater situational awareness, the ability to conduct targeting and deliver effects at range, and the capacity to control multiple assets simultaneously, he added.
Sikorsky screencap The Nomad 100 Fast Pack is built around a standard 20-foot ISO container housing four aircraft, mission-command equipment, communications, power systems, and sustainment supplies.
A promotional video shows the Fast Pack being transported into a combat theater by one of the company’s Black Hawk helicopters as a slung load.

Sikorsky says two Nomad 100s can be prepared for flight “out of the box” in less than 15 minutes and that the other two aircraft — stored on the upper shelf of the container — can be made available within four to six hours.
The package is designed to support runway-independent operations from locations including naval vessels, tactical vehicle staging areas, and improvised landing zones.

As we have discussed in the past , the Nomad 100 combines vertical takeoff and landing with the ability to transition to fixed-wing flight, bringing airplane-like range and endurance to a compact, runway-independent package that can operate from confined locations.

evidenceRecords.text: With both solid rocket boosters fully stacked and all four RS-25 engines now installed on the Core Stage, NASA is preparing to mate the stage to the boosters and form the short stack that will roll to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test.
The test, expected in the coming months, will also give the Artemis III crew their first full launch-day rehearsal on the pad ahead of the targeted no-earlier-than June 2027 mission.

Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems finished stacking the twin five-segment boosters on September 30 by mating the aerodynamic nose cones to the left and right forward assemblies inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at Kennedy Space Center.
The boosters, built by Northrop Grumman, will deliver more than 75 percent of total SLS thrust at liftoff from Pad 39B.
NASA plans to roll the short stack to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test, during which the launch team will practice propellant loading timelines and procedures.

items.title: France mulls keeping Charles de Gaulle carrier sailing after 2038
items.originalTitle: France mulls keeping Charles de Gaulle carrier sailing after 2038
items.summary: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm. Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday. The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm.
Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday.
The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.
As part of an upcoming major refit, France will look into whether the Charles de Gaulle can continue to operate longer, based on the state of onboard systems and the nuclear propulsion, Cluzel said.

With a single carrier, France is without one any time the Charles de Gaulle is in dock for periodic maintenance, and the issue of whether the country needs a second carrier tends to pop up whenever lawmakers question Navy brass.
One obstacle is cost, with the estimated €10 billion budget (US$11.2 billion) for the future France Libre carrier enough to fund at least ten new FDI-class frigates.
Two carriers allow you to maintain a standing alert from Toulon,” Cluzel told the National Assembly’s defense committee, referring to the Charles de Gaulle’s home port in southern France.

He said the future France Libre and the Charles de Gaulle will have two years of overlap in 2036-2038, with two aircraft-carrier crews on active duty, which the Navy chief said is necessary for a seamless transition of skills.

“So from 2036 to 2038 there is a period when the Navy will again have two carriers able to be at sea simultaneously. ”France has said the France Libre will measure 310 meters and displace about 80,000 tonnes, compared to 261.5 meters and 42,000 tons for the Charles de Gaulle.

Studies on extending the Charles de Gaulle’s service life will look at the wear on the reactor cores at the heart of the carrier’s nuclear propulsion system, and the ability to extend operations by keeping fuel on board the carrier for longer, according to Cluzel.

France is committed to limiting its dependencies, and similar to what it did for the steam-powered catapults on the Charles de Gaulle, the country will buy a “substantial” inventory of spare parts for its electromagnetic catapults right at the start of the program, to ensure it can perform repairs independently, according to Cluzel.

evidenceRecords.text: The Royal Navy Type 45 Destroyers appear to have received a new C-UAS system for self protection against drones.
Images released recently by the UK MoD show HMS Dauntless (D33) sporting two mystery containers that are likely acting as interceptor drone launchers.
The Ukrainian Navy ships were closing out Exercise Lion Protector, demonstrating their ability to safely manoeuvre as a small task group in company with a major warship, played by Dauntless.

The apparent lack of new, organic sensors indicate that the interceptors must be receiving targeting data from the Type 45’s existing suite, i.e. the Sampson multi-function radar, the S1850M long-range radar on the aft mast and/or the electro optic systems.
Adapting to new threats The presence of this new system on a Type 45 destroyer shows how navies are adapting to the new challenges posed by affordable drones.
This suggests HMS Dauntless could be the first Type 45 ship to trial the capability ahead of her High North deployment.

Drone attack and swarming tactics—extensively practiced by the Royal Navy and French Navy in dedicated exercises like Sharpshooter and WildFire and based on their experience from Red Sea deployments—highlighted a critical limitation in European navies’ VLS magazine depth (48 cells for Type 45 and Horizon destroyers, 32 cells for French Air Defence FREMMs).
To address this issue, the Royal Navy started transitioning toward DragonFire lasers and C-UAS helicopter (Martlet / LMM aboard Wildcat) .

The new C-UAS system spotted on Dauntless shows that the Royal Navy continues to transform the Type 45 from a conventional air-defence vessel into a highly resilient platform capable of surviving drone saturation.

items.summary: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities. On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command.

evidenceRecords.text: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities.

On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command.

Photo taken during the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre, showing a Corsair USV (left) and the Hellenic Navy-developed Pyrpolitis USV (right).
However, the most notable highlight was a Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vehicle (USV) developed by US company Saronic .
According to a video released by the Ministry of National Defence (screenshots below), at least two Corsair USVs are currently in Greece undergoing trials with the Hellenic Navy.
The trials involved several Fleet units, with the fleet support ships HS Perseas (A377) and possibly HS Aias (A473) serving as motherships for transporting the unmanned vessels.
The trials also demonstrated the vessel’s ability to cooperate tactically with several warships.

Operating from HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Aias On the deck of HS Perseas The Ministry of National Defence stated that the Corsair USVs had undergone extensive trials and had been successfully evaluated by the Hellenic Navy.

A Letter of Request (LOR) has also been submitted to the United States for the procurement of an unspecified number of vessels through the government-to-government Foreign Military Sales (FMS) programme.
Separately, George Sideris of Hellas Journal reports that the Hellenic Navy plans to acquire at least 30 such vessels.
The reported procurement would form part of Greece’s ambition to significantly expand its USV capabilities in the near future.
Corsair USV Specifications The Corsair USV is capable of operating at ranges over 1,000 nautical miles and can support 1,000-pound payloads.

Both systems are part of Northrop’s patented Bushmaster Chain Guns, a collection of medium-caliber, vehicle-mounted machine guns that operate using an external power source.

evidenceRecords.text: With the growing threat of attacks by small unmanned aircraft systems on the battlefield, Northrop Grumman is pitching gun-based air defense systems designed to take down waves of aerial threats.
At the Association of the United States Army’s annual convention, Northrop showed off its newest 50mm Gun-Based Air Defense system dubbed the Raid Hunter and the latest iteration of the M230.
Both systems are part of Northrop’s patented Bushmaster Chain Guns , a collection of medium-caliber, vehicle-mounted machine guns that operate using an external power source.

Kenn Todorov, the company’s vice president and general manager of command and control & weapons integration, called the Raid Hunter “a cost-effective, flexible tool to decisively defeat evolving threats” intended to overwhelm defense systems.

Todorov added that the weapon “addresses a critical short-range defense gap by delivering rapid, high-capacity protection against complex, mass aerial threats like cruise missiles and drone swarms.” Since its introduction in August, the Raid Hunter has completed aeroballistic testing — meaning it was tested against aerial targets — that confirmed pre-test predictions and performance expectations.

Modeled after the M230 gun for Apache attack helicopters, the M230 Link Fed Dual Feed Bushmaster Chain Gun , or M230LF, can be mounted to an assortment of vehicles, ranging from 4x4s to large ground vehicles to patrol boats.

items.summary: Teledyne FLIR Defense has announced the launch of Ranger® R10-3DX, a compact mid-range counter-unmanned aircraft system radar designed to provide advanced drone detection and tracking capabilities for military, security, and critical infrastructure operations. “The Ranger R10-3DX is engineered to support counter-drone, force protection, airport security, border security, coastal surveillance and other critical asset defence missions,” said the company in a press release.

evidenceRecords.text: Teledyne FLIR Defense has announced the launch of Ranger® R10-3DX, a compact mid-range counter-unmanned aircraft system radar designed to provide advanced drone detection and tracking capabilities for military, security, and critical infrastructure operations.

“The Ranger R10-3DX is engineered to support counter-drone, force protection, airport security, border security, coastal surveillance and other critical asset defence missions,” said the company in a press release.
“Using advanced digital beam-forming technology, the R10-3DX provides continuous wide-area coverage and rapid threat detection while maintaining a compact, low size, weight and power footprint.
Ranger R10-3DX can detect micro-UAS targets at ranges exceeding 3 kilometers, pedestrians beyond 6 kilometers, and light vehicles at more than 12 kilometers.

A single radar panel delivers 90-degree azimuth coverage and up to 60 degrees of elevation coverage, while a four-panel configuration provides full 360-degree surveillance.” “Small unmanned aircraft continue to present growing security challenges across military installations, airports, and other key infrastructure sites worldwide,” said Rob Tarantino, Senior Vice President of Surveillance at Teledyne FLIR Defense.

“The Ranger R10-3DX gives operators an affordable, compact, and highly capable radar solution that delivers the early warning and tracking performance needed to counter evolving drone threats.” The Ranger R10-3DX incorporates AI-based target classification algorithms that help users distinguish between drones, aircraft, birds, pedestrians and vehicles, enabling faster and more informed decision-making, says the company.

items.title: SAXON Q Reports That Room-Temperature Quantum Computers Can Rival the Performance of Superconducting Processors
items.originalTitle: SAXON Q Reports That Room-Temperature Quantum Computers Can Rival the Performance of Superconducting Processors
items.summary: Insider Brief SAXON Q reported that its room-temperature diamond quantum computer achieved 77.3% success in a three-qubit Grover search, close to the cited superconducting benchmark of 78%. The system achieved 87% success when searching for two targets among eight items, with both tests exceeding the classical success limits cited in the paper. Researchers conducted the benchmark at Fraunhofer IWU in Dresden using a previous-generation system that consumes roughly 600 watts and requires no cryogenic cooling or vacuum equipment.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SAXON Q reported that its room-temperature diamond quantum computer achieved 77.3% success in a three-qubit Grover search, close to the cited superconducting benchmark of 78%.
The system achieved 87% success when searching for two targets among eight items, with both tests exceeding the classical success limits cited in the paper.
Researchers conducted the benchmark at Fraunhofer IWU in Dresden using a previous-generation system that consumes roughly 600 watts and requires no cryogenic cooling or vacuum equipment.

PRESS RELEASE — — SAXON Q , a leader in NV-center quantum computing, today released a paper showing that its room-temperature diamond-based system can perform on par with superconducting quantum computers cooled to near absolute zero.

Running Grover’s search algorithm, a standard benchmark test for quantum performance, a SAXON Q system identified a single target state 77.3% of the time using three qubits, rivaling the best published superconducting result of 78%, which required a temperature roughly 15,000 times colder.
“The assumption in quantum computing has been that you trade performance for convenience.

“Our system ran a complete quantum algorithm in an ordinary room at a customer site, and the results were similar to those of machines that require extensive infrastructure to cool them to near absolute zero.” Grover’s algorithm — also known as the “quantum search algorithm” — has been used for years to benchmark quantum computers.

It finds a marked item in an unsorted list, using fewer steps than any classical computing method can, and it is a building block for how quantum applications will approach optimization work, financial analysis, cryptography and more.
It uses a sequence that includes the qubits, single and multi-qubit gates, repeated operations and a final readout, all of which work together.

Superconducting quantum computers, by contrast, can demand upwards of 25 kilowatts and must be cooled to near absolute zero inside dilution refrigerators that require specialized facilities and chilled-water cooling.
The experiment was conducted on a previous-generation SAXON Q quantum computer, which predates its new SXQ128 and SXQ512 quantum computers announced in July.
The SXQ128 is available to order now , and SXQ512 deliveries are scheduled to begin in the second quarter of 2027.

PRESS RELEASE — Manipal Institute of Technology, Bengaluru (MIT Bengaluru) on Tuesday launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE.
Venkatesh, VSM (Retd.), 7th Vice Chancellor, MAHE and Advisor to MEMG; Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru; Dr. Karunakar A.

Kotegar, Pro Vice Chancellor, Technology & Science, MAHE; Dr. Raghavendra Prabhu, Additional Registrar, MAHE Bengaluru; Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru; and Mr. Vishal Chatrath, Co-Founder & CEO, QuantrolOX .

Located at the MAHE Bengaluru campus, the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru provides students, researchers and industry collaborators with hands-on access to advanced quantum computing infrastructure, including quantum hardware, cryogenic systems and quantum control technologies.

Through an integrated academic framework, the facility will support experimentation, application development, deep-tech start-up incubation, component innovation, testing and translational research, positioning MIT Bengaluru as an emerging centre for quantum engineering and indigenous hardware development.
The facility commences operations with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system designed for advanced training and experimentation.
Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE, said, “The MAHE House of Quantum at MIT Bengaluru reflects MAHE’s commitment to building advanced scientific capabilities and nurturing talent in emerging technologies.

By creating access to modern quantum infrastructure, we aim to contribute meaningfully to India’s growing quantum ecosystem.” Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru, said, “The Hub brings together education, research and innovation on a common platform.

It will create opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and help translate academic research into real-world technological impact.” Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru, said, “The quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru will provide students and researchers with valuable exposure to real quantum systems and engineering environments.

It marks an important step towards developing the next generation of quantum scientists, engineers and innovators.” Ahead of the launch, faculty members and students from the Bengaluru and Manipal campuses completed specialised training at the MIT Bengaluru campus and the QuantrolOx laboratory at QuTech, TU Delft, in the Netherlands.

The programme developed practical capabilities in dilution refrigerator assembly, cryogenic systems, quantum control technologies, QPU measurements and superconducting quantum hardware, preparing the team to support the operations of the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru.

items.summary: New York City will award NYU $29.2 million to establish a quantum fabrication facility, backed by an additional $255 million from the university and expected to open in 2030. The city will receive three advisory board seats and 15% of NYU Central Administration’s proceeds from intellectual property created using city-funded equipment. The city will receive three advisory board seats and 15% of NYU Central Administration’s proceeds from intellectual property created using city-funded equipment.

PRESS RELEASE — Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani, Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su and New York City Economic Development Corporation (NYCEDC) President and CEO Anthony Shorris announced the city will award $29.2 million to New York University to establish a cutting-edge Quantum Fabrication Facility (QFab), putting New York City at the front of the emerging quantum technology field.

As part of the Mamdani administration’s investment, the city will receive board seats at QFab as well as a stake in new technologies that emerge from QFab, a first-of-its-kind agreement that will allow the City to help shape this emerging technology for the public good.

QFab — which is backed by an additional $255 million investment from NYU spanning construction and 10 years of operations — will give researchers, students, start-ups and established companies access to specialized equipment for building and testing new quantum devices.
It is expected to support more than 100 companies and reach 35,000 New Yorkers in its first 10 years of operation.

Additionally, to grow the number of New York City jobs in the quantum field, NYU will provide students at the City University of New York (CUNY) and New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) with access to state-of-the-art labs, training, new certificate programs and summer workshops.

Altogether, today’s announcement represents a historic investment by the Mamdani administration in the future of New York City’s economy and helps set a new national model for economic development for the public good.

“Providing New York City students, researchers, and companies with access to a Quantum Fabrication Facility (QFab) and specialized equipment through NYU will allow our City to engage, shape, and grow with this emerging technology,” said Assemblymember Deborah Glick.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army announced that it is awarding initial contracts to several defense technology companies to build applications for its new battlefield software.
The service will pay a one-year total of $93.6 million, spread out across nine companies, to create applications for its Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, software.

The NGC2 system, in conjunction with the applications the companies build for it, will allow information sharing that streamlines mission completion across the Army’s six warfighting functions of command and control, fires, intelligence, movement and maneuver, sustainment and protection, the service said.

“While the Army is providing capability we can deploy today, we’re also providing a blueprint and reference point for how industry can integrate in the future with interoperability and speed,” said Brig.
Gen. Shane Taylor, portfolio management executive for the Command and Control Information Network.
The NGC2 will provide a shared network for technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications to operate within that will increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.
The chosen companies include General Dynamics Mission Systems, Air Space Intelligence Federal, Immersive Wisdom, LMI, Mente Systems, Stilman Advanced Strategies, Onebrief, Rune Technologies and AIR.

items.originalTitle: Estonia weighs buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones
items.summary: VIENNA — Estonia’s new defense minister said his country should consider buying light jet aircraft to shoot down Russia’s faster, jet-powered attack drones. Martin Herem, a retired general who took office Sept. 16, floated the idea in interviews after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. He told The Baltic Sentinel and the daily Postimees that Estonia should study the option, saying air-to-air weapons are the most effective counter to the drones. Herem has not committed to buying anything.

He told The Baltic Sentinel and the daily Postimees that Estonia should study the option, saying air-to-air weapons are the most effective counter to the drones.
Martin Herem, a retired general who took office Sept. 16, floated the idea in interviews after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv.
Herem has not committed to buying anything.
He told The Baltic Sentinel he is also looking at computer-controlled cannons, heavy machine guns and fast, jet-powered interceptor drones.
He noted that Estonia already has pilots, air-control expertise and L-39 trainers.
The two L-39 Albatros trainers Estonia uses are leased, according to the Estonian military’s website.
Their civilian status and lease terms would complicate any move to arm them, the former head of Estonia’s air force said back in April.
The proposal responds to a threat that is growing fast.
Yuriy Ihnat, a Ukrainian air force spokesman, said Ukraine intercepted about 40% of jet-powered drones in July and 60% in August, according to Hromadske.
In the same period, the number of jet-powered drones fired at Ukraine increased from a few hundred to several thousands a month.
Ukraine’s defense ministry puts their speed at more than 400 kilometers per hour.

evidenceRecords.text: HD Hyundai Heavy Industries has launched BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries press release Marking another milestone in a decade-long defense partnership, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) launched the BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy, at its primary shipyard in Ulsan on Monday.
The ceremonial launching—HD HHI’s first export naval vessel launch of the year—was attended by prominent diplomatic and military leaders from both nations, including Vice Admiral Jose Ma.
Ambrosio Ezpeleta, Flag Officer in Command of the Philippine Navy; Bernadette Therese Fernandez, Philippine Ambassador to South Korea; Lieutenant General Rommel P.
Roldan, Vice Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines; and Won-ho Joo, President & Head of Naval & Medium Size Ships Business Unit at HD HHI.
Named after the 16th-century ruler of Cebu who played a pivotal role in early Philippine history, the Rajah Humabon is scheduled for official delivery in February 2027.
BRP Rajah Humabon launching ceremony.

Advanced Maritime Capabilities Designed to enhance maritime domain awareness and coastal defense capabilities across the Philippine archipelago, the state-of-the-art 2,400-ton vessel measures 94 meters in length and 14 meters in width.

Capable of maintaining a cruising speed of 15 knots (approximately 28 km/h) with an impressive operational range of 5,500 nautical miles (10,186 km), the patrol ship is built for extended endurance at sea.
The vessel is equipped with advanced defense systems, including a 76mm main naval gun, a 30mm secondary gun, decoy launching systems, surveillance radar, and electro-optical tracking equipment.
A Decade of Naval Partnership The launch of the Rajah Humabon marks a decade of continuous naval cooperation between HD HHI and the Philippine Armed Forces.
The relationship began in 2016 with a milestone contract for the Philippine Navy’s first modern frigates.

In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issued its first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.
Two months later, Israel has still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter.
Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.
A Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment.
The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined to comment.
Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved.
He listed it again last week in a screed on social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.
The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.

Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter.
The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.
The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said.
Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.

items.title: Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
items.originalTitle: Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
items.summary: The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW . State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away.

evidenceRecords.text: The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW .

State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away.
Some also note that federal workforce departures have weakened cooperation with outside partners, including social media platforms, to track false information online.

While the federal government continues to gather intelligence on foreign threats to U.S. elections, some of those who lean on those findings say federal agencies are less reliably sharing information with non-federal researchers and state officials responsible for countering those campaigns.
That cooperation began to weaken before President Donald Trump returned to office, and his administration has since dismantled several programs dedicated to countering the problem.
This story is based on interviews with current and former federal officials, state election officials and specialists in cybersecurity and influence operations.

Their concerns come as fast-evolving AI tools now allow foreign influence operators to do more than just generate fake images or audio, instead helping them produce plausible-sounding messages, find audiences to target and autonomously adjust campaigns at a scale not seen before.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions about foreign malign influence to the Justice Department, saying that influence operations fall outside CISA’s mission.
“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration, DHS, and CISA,” a CISA spokesperson said.
Foreign influence operations aim to shape what people believe and how they act, often without revealing who is behind the message.

evidenceRecords.text: Credit: NASA NASA will preview two upcoming spacewalks to complete solar array installation and power augmentation of the International Space Station during a news conference at 2 p.m.
EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 20, from NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live NASA participants in the news conference include: Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager, Low Earth Orbit Program Garrett Hehn, spacewalk flight director, Flight Operations Directorate United States-based media interested in attending in person must contact the Johnson newsroom no later than 3 p.m., Monday, Oct. 19, at: jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov .

Thursday, Oct. 29 During U.S. spacewalk 100, NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk will exit the station’s Quest airlock to install and deploy an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the 2A electrical power channel.
The solar array will be the seventh IROSA and will provide additional power to support critical station operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit.
Thursday, Nov. 5 During U.S. spacewalk 101, Menon and Kutryk will install and deploy the eighth and final IROSA on the 3B channel of the space station, completing the power augmentation upgrades.
The final two roll-out solar arrays will complete the space station’s power system augmentation.
Together, the eight roll-out arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s electric power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.
NASA will share additional coverage details about U.S. spacewalks 100 and 101 closer to each operation on the agency’s live events web page and the space station blog .
The spacewalks will be the 285th and 286th conducted in support of space station assembly, maintenance, and upgrades.

items.originalTitle: Oshkosh adapts JLTV for Dutch military patrol vehicle
items.summary: Wisconsin-based Oshkosh Defense has begun production of the first prototype of the Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle, or DXPV. According to the company, the new vehicle, also called the “Kaaiman,” was derived from the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle , or JLTV, and adapted for the Netherlands Ministry of Defence .

evidenceRecords.text: Wisconsin-based Oshkosh Defense has begun production of the first prototype of the Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle, or DXPV.
According to the company, the new vehicle, also called the “Kaaiman,” was derived from the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle , or JLTV, and adapted for the Netherlands Ministry of Defence .

At the 2026 AUSA Annual Meeting and Exposition, Pat Williams, the company’s chief program officer, described the “production” as “an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands.” Compared to a standard JLTV, the DXPV has been enhanced for mobility, corrosion protection, mission systems and suspension for increased off-road performance.

“Just as importantly, it demonstrates the strength of an active production base and our ability to continuously evolve proven vehicle technologies to address the changing needs of our customers and their missions,” Williams said.

Beyond the DXPV prototype, Oshkosh officials at the show are emphasizing the company’s renewed approach toward “rapidly delivering mission-ready solutions.” The company added that it has delivered more than 200,000 tactical wheeled vehicles to U.S. and allied forces.
The Oshkosh AUSA booth also featured other platforms like its Family of Medium Tactical Vehicle A2 Low-Velocity Air Drop, or FMTV A2 LVAD, and the hybrid electric JLTV, or simply eJLTV.
With that, Williams added that “production readiness matters,” referring to how quickly Oshkosh was able to develop the DXPV.
The Dutch MoD signed an agreement with Oshkosh for the vehicles last summer and then placed an order valued between $25 and $30 million in January.
“Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development,” Williams said.

items.summary: In a new paper in Nature , the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks. “Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says.

“It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and

Longer forecasts In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes.

“He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says.

items.title: US Army expands drone marketplace to 33 nations
items.originalTitle: US Army expands drone marketplace to 33 nations
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally. Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s online marketplace for rapid drone acquisition is expanding internationally.

Representatives of Canada, Croatia, Egypt, Japan, Kuwait, Morocco, Albania and Panama signed a statement of intent to join the Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Marketplace during a ceremony Tuesday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Robert Brown, president and CEO of AUSA, said that the signing brought the total number of participating nations to 33.
The marketplace was launched in March 2026 with nine European signers and continues to grow across regional allies and partners.
“With today’s signing, the marketplace is now truly a global effort,” said Brent Ingraham, assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology.
More recently, the Army awarded counter-UAS contract vehicles worth $7 billion through the marketplace, Ingraham said.
The Army also operates a C-UAS Marketplace developed and operated by the Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF 401) for digital procurement of counter-drone systems.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, who attended the signing ceremony, said the drone marketplace was “connecting soldiers directly with builders and removing the bureaucratic middlemen.” Telle’s comments follow a Monday address to AUSA where he touted Army efforts to streamline acquisition.
The acting secretary further emphasized that the global drone marketplace builds on the Army’s demand for open architecture systems.

Telle said the Army needs to elevate open architectures beyond the tactical systems to “the strategic level,” saying the drone marketplace is a “great step forward” in sharing tactics, techniques, procedures and equipment with partners.

items.summary: Sikorsky is aiming to start offering a new modular and readily swappable nose for the venerable H-60 family of helicopters within the next year or so. The noses will be made available on new-production H-60s, as well as be retrofittable to helicopters in service now. The ‘nose jobs’ will help operators relatively quickly reconfigure their H-60s for very different missions, from cargo-carrying to serving as gunships , as required.

Our Howard Altman had a chance to speak with representatives from Sikorsky, now a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin, about the plans for the new nose for the H-60-series at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention today.
Within the next, I would say, year or so, the nose will be available to be retrofitted or to be coming off the line,” Jason Wrigley, Sikorsky’s director of business development for Black Hawk, said.

“The new modular nose will change the look of the Black Hawk up front to provide even more space for equipment that will work directly with the new digital architecture.” In terms of swapping out modular noses on individual helicopters, Wrigley said that it is still too early in the design process to know exactly how that would be done and how long it might take to do so in practice.

PRESS RELEASE — Bristol-based Siloton has been awarded a major contract to accelerate the development of its groundbreaking handheld eye imaging system, which makes the detection and monitoring of retinal diseases more accessible to patients.
The med-tech start-up has secured £8.4 million from Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), through its Contracts for Innovation: Quantum Missions Primer initiative.

Delivered over two years, the contract will help Siloton accelerate the design of the in-clinic and at-home versions of its GiraffeOCT optical coherence tomography (OCT) device, as well as complete trials on both systems.
The start-up expects the funding could cut the development process by up to two years.

Siloton will work with Sunderland Specialist Eye Hospital on clinical trials over the course of the contract for its in-clinic device, giving patients across the North East and North Cumbria access to the technology during its development.

The programme helps public sector organisations to solve some of their most complex challenges by running competitive funding opportunities for the development of new technologies.
York Health Economics Consortium will also use this data to refine their cost-saving-estimates for the NHS.
The project will create a number of high-skilled jobs during the next two years, with the Siloton team expected to grow to 16 by August 2028.
The roles will support the miniaturisation of the systems’ electronics, product development, and manufacturing plans, across specialisms including photonics, electronics, and software development.

The company is planning to raise further investment off the back of the contract win, strengthening its cash position for the next few years and supporting the development of its second-generation CheetahOCT device, specifically designed to measure different layers of the retina and expand the number of conditions it can detect.

items.originalTitle: QFX Wins £6.8 Million Innovate UK Contract for Quantum Timing Hardware
items.summary: Insider Brief QFX, an Oxford University spinout, has secured a £6.8 million Innovate UK contract to develop atomic and vacuum hardware for data centre timing and space applications. The SrROCK Phase II programme will build a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock package, demonstrate its timing performance and conduct testing relevant to future satellite missions. The programme aims to establish UK manufacturing capacity and intellectual property for advanced atomic and vacuum systems while supporting QFX’s development of distributed quantum computing and networking hardware.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief QFX, an Oxford University spinout, has secured a £6.8 million Innovate UK contract to develop atomic and vacuum hardware for data centre timing and space applications.
The SrROCK Phase II programme will build a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock package, demonstrate its timing performance and conduct testing relevant to future satellite missions.

The programme aims to establish UK manufacturing capacity and intellectual property for advanced atomic and vacuum systems while supporting QFX’s development of distributed quantum computing and networking hardware.

PRESS RELEASE — QFX (Quantum Fabrix Ltd), an Oxford University spinout developing hardware infrastructure for distributed quantum computing and quantum networking, has been awarded a £6.8 million contract by Innovate UK to deliver Phase II of its SrROCK development programme.
Building on a successful first phase, SrROCK will advance QFX’s atomic source and vacuum technologies into robust, integrated hardware for data centre and space applications.
QFX’s technology platform combines atomic sources, ultra-high-vacuum systems and quantum interfaces in a modular architecture for demanding data centre and space applications.
This approach gives QFX access to near-term opportunities in timing and navigation while building towards fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.
“SrROCK gives QFX the opportunity to prove that its core atomic and vacuum technologies can be manufactured and qualified for demanding real-world applications.

That capability is essential to scaling our quantum-computing platform and creates a clear route into the strategically important timing market, supporting sovereign UK supply of advanced timing technology.” Dr Timothy Ballance , CEO, QFX In Phase II, QFX will engineer and integrate a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock physics package for timing infrastructure in data centres and future satellite missions.
The programme will demonstrate timing performance and complete space-relevant testing, generating the evidence needed for customer adoption and future space qualification.

Engagement with data centre operators, spacecraft manufacturers, mission operators and end users will define deployment requirements, commercial pathways and plans for a subsequent space demonstration.

items.summary: Insider Brief INmune Bio and Quantum Computing Inc . are collaborating to use quantum optimization, AI and biomedical data analytics to identify potential new applications for INmune Bio’s investigational treatment XPro. The collaboration will compare quantum optimization results with conventional statistical and machine-learning methods, and represents QCi’s first commercial engagement in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology market. evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief INmune Bio and Quantum Computing Inc . are collaborating to use quantum optimization, AI and biomedical data analytics to identify potential new applications for INmune Bio’s investigational treatment XPro.

The collaboration will compare quantum optimization results with conventional statistical and machine-learning methods, and represents QCi’s first commercial engagement in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology market.

PRESS RELEASE — INmune Bio Inc. (Nasdaq: INMB ) and Quantum Computing Inc. (Nasdaq: QUBT ) today announced a collaboration to apply quantum computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to identify new potential applications for XPro (XPro1595), INmune Bio’s investigational treatment for Alzheimer’s disease and other disease conditions.
The collaboration brings together INmune Bio’s data from pre-clinical research through four clinical trials and understanding of disease biology with QCi’s Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine.
“We’ve built a large clinical dataset on Alzheimer’s and other diseases, backed by years of work with XPro,” said David Moss, Chief Executive Officer of INmune Bio.

We’ll look for the diseases with the greatest potential for success, those whose human biology matches what we’ve already seen XPro do, starting with rare diseases where trials can be smaller, faster and more capital-efficient, and where qualifying pediatric approvals may earn a Priority Review Voucher.” Together, the companies will build on INmune Bio’s research into XPro to explore where its approach to targeting inflammation may offer the greatest potential.

Using its Dirac-3S entropy quantum optimization machine alongside AI and conventional analytics, QCi will look for patterns and relationships across these datasets that could help researchers better understand treatment responses, identify promising patient populations and prioritize new indications for further study.

The potential to help researchers make better decisions about future treatments is exciting, and it opens an important new market for QCi.” An important part of the program will be testing where quantum optimization adds value.

The companies plan to compare results from QCi’s quantum optimization machine with appropriate conventional statistical and machine-learning methods, evaluating which approaches are best suited to different parts of the analysis.
The work is also intended to establish a repeatable discovery process through quantum computing that INmune Bio can use with additional datasets and potential disease indications.
For INmune Bio, the collaboration offers a new way to evaluate the broader potential of XPro and prioritize future development opportunities.

items.title: DroneShield announces Q4 software update for counter-drone systems
items.originalTitle: DroneShield announces Q4 software update for counter-drone systems
items.summary: DroneShield has announced a fourth-quarter software release designed to improve drone detection, identification, tracking and defeat capabilities across its counter-unmanned aircraft systems. The update introduces a feature that flags unfamiliar radio-frequency signals exhibiting drone-like characteristics, allowing operators to investigate potential new threats that are not yet included in DroneShield’s threat library. It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.

evidenceRecords.text: DroneShield has announced a fourth-quarter software release designed to improve drone detection, identification, tracking and defeat capabilities across its counter-unmanned aircraft systems.
It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.
The release also enables radio-frequency sensors and compatible optical cameras to work together for passive detection and visual confirmation.
With compatible Bosch Starlight cameras, operators can direct cameras towards the source of an RF detection before locking on to and tracking a drone.

For threat mitigation, connected DroneSentry-X Mk2 units can share detections to coordinate disruption, while jamming can be focused on frequencies used by the specific drone to reduce interference with nearby systems.

DroneShield said the software is available through its Mission Ready Services subscription, enabling compatible equipment already in the field to receive capability improvements without new hardware investment.
The DroneSentry-C2 software release is scheduled to become available on 3 November 2026.

items.title: Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close
items.originalTitle: Google says self-improving AI isn't anywhere close
items.summary: Google engineer Haydn Belfield says self-improving AI remains far off, even as significant automation is already taking hold. Google Deepmind has seen no measurable acceleration of AI research driven by AI itself, according to Belfield. That doesn't mean significant automation isn't happening already: AI now writes more than 75 percent of production code. But about 88 percent of code changes still need human oversight or review, and every change is reviewed by a human before submission, according to Belfield. The share of code changes fully delegated to AI rose from 7.5 to 11.9 percent.

evidenceRecords.text: A month after President Donald Trump intervened to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea, citing a desire not to upset his “very good relationship” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, the commander of Army forces on the peninsula said he’d like to go bigger – both in exercise frequency and geographic scope.

Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“I think what we recognize is that largely the two big exercises every year in Korea focus on large command posts; we’ve got to move away from that,” Brunson said, in response to a question from a Korean journalist.

Speaking at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting here Monday, Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of United Nations Command, Combined Forces Command, and United States Forces Korea, said lessons from Ukraine prompted interest in changing the shape and structure of exercises there.

“So, what we intend to do is take advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight,” he continued. “We’re trying to say how might we train differently, and so [Gen. Kim Sung-min, deputy commander of the Republic of Korea–U.S. Combined Forces Command] and I talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion.”

In light of the distributed fight and scope of battle in Ukraine, Brunson suggested a training exercise that spanned from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province — a distance of nearly 300 miles across nearly the full span of the Korean peninsula.

“Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say, ‘You can’t utilize the things that you’ve learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learn the same lessons and we’ve distributed ourselves in such a way that we don’t make ourselves the target,” he said.

The library supports tools including Qiskit, PennyLane, NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket, alongside hardware from IBM and IQM, and includes algorithms for quantum machine learning, optimization, chemistry and finance.

PRESS RELEASE — EigenOrbit has released eigenkit, a free open-source Python library for quantum computing.
With eigenkit, a quantum algorithm is written once and runs on a simulator on an ordinary laptop or on real quantum computers from IBM, IQM and the vendors available through Amazon Braket.
Quantum teams today often pick a simulator or a hardware vendor first and then write code against that vendor’s SDK.
EigenOrbit uses eigenkit as the foundation of its own platform for comparing quantum and classical approaches on industrial problems.

EigenOrbit has released eigenkit 1.0, a free, open-source Python library designed to run quantum algorithms across multiple simulators and quantum hardware platforms without rewriting the algorithm for each backend.
Moving from one machine to another takes a single setting, and the rest of the code stays as it was.
Yet no single backend suits every workload.

Quantum processors differ in qubit count, connectivity, native gates, error rates, price and queue times, so the best device can change from one circuit to the next. eigenkit separates the definition of an algorithm from the machine that executes it, which makes trying several backends a routine step.
Many machines, one codebase. eigenkit runs on its own built-in simulator and on PennyLane, Qiskit, Qiskit Aer, Qulacs, qsim, TensorCircuit, NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket simulators.
On hardware it supports IBM quantum computers, IQM quantum computers and the processors available on Amazon Braket.
Photonic circuits run through Quandela’s Perceval.
Familiar tools. eigenkit works with PyTorch and scikit-learn, the libraries most data scientists already use.
The library comes from a team that has built quantum software for industrial clients in finance, energy, healthcare and manufacturing for more than five years.

PRESS RELEASE — Today, IBM (NYSE: IBM ), in collaboration with Siemens, announced new research aimed at advancing IBM’s nanostack architecture , a new transistor architecture unveiled by IBM earlier this year.

The collaboration will bring together IBM’s leadership in semiconductor device innovation and Siemens’ expertise in electronic design automation (EDA), process simulation, lithography optimization, and advanced manufacturing software to accelerate the development of nanostack.

Through this collaboration, IBM and Siemens will work to advance the design, simulation, and lithography techniques needed for this and future nanostack generations beyond the current 7 angstrom node.
The collaboration includes developing advanced virtual models of nanostack in order to model performance, optimize designs, and address fabrication challenges before chips are built.

“We are thrilled to work with Siemens as we continue to advance this technology and explore new approaches to extend angstrom-level scaling with nanostack.” “Scaling semiconductors into the angstrom era demands tightly coupled co-optimization between device physics, EDA design and manufacturing software, and manufacturing.

As physical AI places extraordinary demands on silicon architecture, IBM ‘s 3D nanostack design represents a pivotal leap forward,” said Ankur Gupta, Executive Vice President, EDA IC Portfolio, Siemens .

“Siemens’ collaboration with IBM to advance virtual modeling, simulation, lithography, and design software optimizations needed to address physical limitations early and accelerate the development of these complex architectures is truly pioneering.” By combining IBM ‘s semiconductor leadership with Siemens’ advanced EDA software and simulation technologies, the companies aim to accelerate technology development cycles and advance the manufacturing foundation necessary for bringing nanostack toward production.

items.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.originalTitle: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
items.summary: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol. The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

evidenceRecords.text: Wolk Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.
The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

An explanation for the Treble Clef has been particularly difficult to find because the formation lies almost directly behind the plane of the Milky Way, meaning that stars, gas, and dust from our home galaxy largely block the view from Earth.

NASA’s Chandra and the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) X-ray telescope found diffuse, hot gas at the location of the Treble Clef, showing that a galaxy cluster hosts the object.
The researchers also determined the galaxy cluster is, in fact, two clusters in the process of merging.
Galaxy clusters are some of the largest structures in the universe, containing hundreds of individual galaxies and huge reservoirs of superheated gas.

This new composite image of the Treble Clef and its cluster shows the multimillion-degree gas detected in X-rays by Chandra and eROSITA in blue, with some of the Chandra data derived from a special technique the authors used to highlight important features in the Chandra data.
Radio data shown in red from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), a large network of radio telescopes in Europe reveals the doppelganger of the musical notation.
The final piece of the combined image comes from infrared data obtained by the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, appearing mostly white.
The authors concluded that the Treble Clef likely formed in a two-stage process.
First, an earlier outburst from a supermassive black hole in the galaxy cluster’s center drove clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away at close to the speed of light.
This led to a type of cosmic crescendo and initially produced bright radio waves that later faded as the particles lost energy.

items.summary: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab. evidenceRecords.text: BASE AERONAVAL CRISTÓBAL COLÓN, Panama — Though many service members venture into the hot, humid terrain of the U.S. Army’s jungle school in Panama , not all leave with the newly authorized-for-wear Jungle tab.
The Panama course, back after a decades-long hiatus, resumed in 2025 as the U.S. military shifted its focus to the Western Hemisphere.
In August, the Army confirmed it had approved the small arch-shaped patch — emblazoned with the word “Jungle” — for service-wide wear on the left shoulder.

Those who attended the course from 1990 to 1999 at Fort Sherman, now known as Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, are authorized the tab retroactively , as well as those who attended the 12-day jungle school in Oahu, Hawaii, after Fort Sherman’s closure.

The 18-day course includes classes on flora, fauna, machetes, jungle first aid, fire-starting, shelter-building, and more, but showing up and trudging through muddy terrain in crippling Panama humidity is not enough to earn the tab.
“There’s a difference between graduating the course with the tab and finishing the course,” said Lt.
Andrew Eagan, the officer in charge of the Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama, or JOTC-P.
Even if students fail one part of the curriculum, as long as their failure presents no medical or safety issues, they must finish the course.
There are then five critical tasks across the course that you have to pass in order to graduate with the tab,” Eagen said.
Combat Water Survival Assessment and 5K Early in the course, participants face physical fitness tests.

The Combat Water Survival Assessment, or CWSA, requires participants to complete a variety of survival tasks in the water, including swimming in combat gear, ditching their equipment and dropping from a meters-high diving board.
The 5-kilometer run — only 3.1 miles — has proven one of the course’s toughest obstacles for many jungle school candidates.

items.title: AI drone outpaces former world champions using one camera and no GPS
items.originalTitle: AI drone outpaces former world champions using one camera and no GPS
items.summary: What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots? At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes. Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera. It outperformed even former world champion human drone pilots in a race.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have developed an AI system that enables a racing drone to navigate demanding courses at extreme speed using only a single camera.
It outperformed even former world champion human drone pilots in a race.
What does it take for an autonomous robot to be faster around a course than human drone pilots?
At these dizzying speeds, humans need lightning-fast reflexes.

Now published in Science Robotics, the scientific work behind this accomplishment shows how compact, efficient neural-network-based control can achieve high-performance autonomous flight under real-world conditions.
The underlying principles could help advance a much broader class of autonomous robots, from vehicles to mobile and humanoid systems.
The TU Delft team set out to investigate how far artificial intelligence can push a drone with very limited sensors, onboard computing power and energy.
This is a challenging problem: at high speed, even a small delay in sensing or control can mean missing a gate, colliding with an obstacle or losing control and crashing.
At high speed, the drone has very little time to interpret what it sees.
A neural network identifies the racing gates in the camera images, while the onboard IMU and a model of the drone estimate its position and motion.
The system does all this without GPS or external motion tracking.

"We developed a robust way of combining what the camera sees with the drone's own motion information, allowing it to navigate the track at high speed without GPS." The system also had to cope with imperfections that occur in real flight, including camera interference and sensor saturation.
For Guido de Croon, professor at Delft University of Technology, the value of drone racing goes beyond making drones fly faster.
In the current study, we made an AI efficient enough to control a drone traveling at 100 kilometers per hour (62 miles per hour) using a single camera and a small onboard processor.

items.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
items.originalTitle: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
items.summary: Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on. Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare. Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming. But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official.

evidenceRecords.text: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare.
Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.
But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official.
Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.

Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.

Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."
Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes.
There is no ready replacement for the network.
Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.

Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories and Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology published a technical paper titled “Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations.”
“Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs) are emerging as successors to Fin Field-Effect Transistors (FinFETs) and are central to continued scaling at advanced semiconductor nodes.

Despite their improved electrostatic control, recent measurements show that the drain current in GAAFETs deviates strongly from thermionic behavior at negative gate voltages, increasing as the gate voltage becomes more negative.
This leakage has been attributed to direct gate-drain tunneling through the high-k dielectric, enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering (DIDBL).

Here, we use predictive, charge-self-consistent Non-Equilibrium Green Function (NEGF) simulations based on the Contact Block Reduction (CBR) method to spatially resolve this leakage pathway in GAAFETs.”

Extensive Network SRL today announced a strategic commercial agreement to build quantum application development, education, enterprise and national capabilities at the campus’s hardware-enabled Quantum AI center in Iași, Romania.
Under the agreement, FreeYa Mind Campus will offer access to Classiq ’s enterprise-grade quantum software platform , both on campus and across the Romanian ecosystem.

The platform brings together Classiq’s agentic AI interfaces, Qmod high-level modeling language, circuit synthesis and hardware-aware execution, helping researchers and enterprise teams design optimized quantum applications faster.
The initiative will draw on FreeYa Mind Campus’s network of enterprises, research institutions, public-sector organizations and academic partners, including more than 12 partner universities.
Working with the campus team, Classiq will connect quantum innovation to real-world industry applications.
The campus will offer university curriculum materials, practitioner training, enterprise onboarding, advanced application development and Classiq certification resources.
To support customer engagement, project execution and application delivery, Classiq will establish its Romania regional headquarters at the campus.

By combining Classiq ’s software engineering platform and education with FreeYa Mind Campus’s quantum infrastructure, the partnership strengthens the Romanian and wider European quantum ecosystems, developing the skills, workflows and applications needed to put that infrastructure to effective use.

Building on the success of FreeYa Mind Campus, we are bringing those elements together, and Classiq will provide the scalable software foundation that lets universities, enterprises and public institutions develop quantum applications,” said Regev Yativ , CRO at Classiq.

evidenceRecords.text: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) has developed a new tool that uses neuromorphic cameras to detect unmanned aerial system (UAS) drones.
SwRI's Hierax system pairs event-based cameras, dynamic sensing technology that mimics the power of human eyesight, with custom software to detect fast-moving drones in complex aerial scenarios.

"Our approach potentially transforms any UAS into an autonomous precision interceptor designed to detect, track, pursue and neutralize rogue or hostile drones without manual piloting," said Kase Saylor, an SwRI research manager. "By leveraging neuromorphic sensing, we provide a hardware-agnostic intercept kit that bridges the gap between detection and neutralization."
The evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine has demonstrated a critical need for counter-UAS technologies to support the U.S. military and its allies.
Drones are commonly detected using radar, radio frequency signals, acoustics, thermal imaging or optical cameras.
Event-based, or neuromorphic, cameras offer advantages because they do not emit signals that can be jammed by adversaries while offering reduced size, weight, power and costs.

Neuromorphic cameras capture even slight changes in brightness at the pixel level, much like biological eyesight, unlike optical cameras that only capture individual frames of light in red, green and blue wavelengths.
Although event-based cameras have been a topic of interest in laboratory research for decades, they have only recently been adapted to operate in complex environments.
The SwRI solution requires less computing power than standard optical sensing systems that rely on complex machine learning.

"By keeping up with the latest research and applying it to real-world applications, we are committed to helping our clients leverage the latest advancements in technology, such as neuromorphic cameras," said David Anthony, an SwRI engineer who led the research.
SwRI used a modular open systems approach to develop the Hierax imaging package to meet U.S. Department of Defense requirements for battlefield interoperability across combined joint task forces.
