evidenceRecords.text: Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic .

The team focused on different configurations of thermal wrappings, insulation and other components to ensure that parts of the kit’s components that are particularly vulnerable to cracking and freezing — hoses, valves, bladders and pumps — were able to withstand the greater threshold for cold, according to a recent Army release.

“Our armed forces live and operate in extremely cold and difficult conditions, so having these facilities operational is important for their physical and mental health while serving in the Arctic and other high-north environments,” said Dr. Dan Tague, a research chemist at CRREL, one of seven U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center laboratories.
Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic.
As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1.

Which is why the Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, or NAVFAC EXWC, and the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory, or CRREL, began working with both branches to field a rapidly deployable Triple Container rigid-wall shelter system usable in temperatures as low as -50 degrees Fahrenheit.
The already fielded version can operate in temperatures as low as -15 degrees Fahrenheit.
The result, per the release, far exceeded the objectives, with the TRICON-based system staying operational down to -65 degrees Fahrenheit.
Testing took place in CRREL’s New Hampshire-based Extreme Cold Chamber, a 288-square-foot cold room capable of reaching temperatures as low as -90 degrees Fahrenheit, per the release.

While military units typically have to wait until the Alaskan winter reaches its peak to simulate similar conditions, the controlled environment allowed the research team to create conditions similar to those of the real world.

items.title: Drones on the line: New algorithms help drone fleets inspect power infrastructure
items.originalTitle: Drones on the line: New algorithms help drone fleets inspect power infrastructure
items.summary: Researchers have developed two algorithms to help fleets of drones inspect electricity infrastructure more efficiently, potentially cutting costs and reducing risks to human workers. They provide details in the International Journal of Systems, Control and Communications. The work offers solutions to two inspection tasks. The first is checking individual components on power transmission towers, such as insulators, and the second is surveying transmission lines for hazards.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers have developed two algorithms to help fleets of drones inspect electricity infrastructure more efficiently, potentially cutting costs and reducing risks to human workers.
They provide details in the International Journal of Systems, Control and Communications.
The work offers solutions to two inspection tasks.
The first is checking individual components on power transmission towers, such as insulators, and the second is surveying transmission lines for hazards.

If unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), drones, are to be used for these two tasks, then multiple drones operating from a single base to cover routes would be optimal, but there is a need to minimize total flight distance.
For component inspections, the researchers developed an improved genetic algorithm.
This is a computational method inspired by natural selection that progressively refines possible solutions.
It combines a technique called 2-opt, which improves routes by reversing sections of a flight path, with an adaptive mutation rate.
Mutations introduce changes into the possible solutions, which helps the algorithm to avoid poor routes.
For transmission-line inspections, the team developed a separate adaptive genetic algorithm to allocate line segments among drones and minimize unnecessary travel.
Tests on maps of different sizes compared its performance with a conventional genetic algorithm.
These showed improvements in solution quality and efficiency over earlier approaches.

items.title: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
items.originalTitle: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
items.summary: Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran. The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November. The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.

Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.

On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
The Singapore-flagged ​container ‌ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day.
Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a ​projectile ​on 23 September, according to data from ‌the ‌International Maritime Organization.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.

The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), a leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced the pricing of a $2.0 billion equity offering.

“This investment will accelerate the commercialization of our full-stack quantum platform and is a tremendous vote of confidence in the trailblazing innovation that has defined IonQ ,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“The significance of this raise goes beyond its size — giving IonQ additional strategic flexibility as the best-capitalized pure-play quantum company.

Our advancement to Stage C of DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative and NVIDIA partnership are both significant votes of confidence in our near-term technology roadmap.” De Masi continued, “With Q-Day quickly approaching, we are investing to advance the long-term path to profitability of our full-stack quantum computing, networking, sensing and security platform.

IonQ is positioned to create strong value for shareholders by helping customers protect themselves today as we lead the way to manufacturing and deploying utility-scale quantum computing.” The offering consists of 20,500,000 shares of IonQ ’s common stock, each at $40.00 per share, and pre-funded warrants to purchase 29,500,000 shares of IonQ’s common stock, each at $40.00 per pre-funded warrant, each representing a premium of approximately 15% to IonQ’s closing stock price on October 13, 2026, as well as seven-year warrants to purchase 100,000,000 additional shares of IonQ’s common stock,
The securities offered will be purchased from the underwriter by an entity managed by Heights Capital Management, Inc. (the “investor”).

items.originalTitle: Characterization of HBM Power Consumption (ETH Zurich, NYU)
items.summary: Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” Abstract Excerpt: “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips.

Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips.

Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant.

Leveraging our empirical insights into HBM2 power consumption, we engineer an access pattern that yields 23.6% higher power consumption on average across 36 tested HBM2 chips than the highest-power-consuming JEDEC-specified current measurement loop.” Find the technical paper here .

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW — With Poland only partway through an air defense modernization effort, the Polish Air Force has been operating at the highest readiness on a nightly basis, which is putting heavy strain on personnel and equipment, according to Maj.
Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, the operational commander for the Polish Armed Forces.
Nowak said 80 percent of his service’s attention is focused on air defense, with the ground and air components of Poland’s integrated air defenses still three to four years away.
In the meantime, the Air Force has changed how it operates in order to fill the gap.
Starting Oct. 1, the service stopped following Visual Identification (VID) procedures in which a pilot confirms a target’s type, markings or nationality by sight before engaging.
“So now we are much more flexible, much more responsive,” Nowak, who is responsible for Polish airspace, said.

During the panel discussion, Nowak acknowledged that using fighter jets to shoot down cheap drones is a bad cost ratio for Poland, but said there simply isn’t any other option at the moment. “We need to develop massive, responsive weapons systems capable to counter-react the UAVs operations,” he said.
Poland should have some options, but systems that the country hoped to have ready now are still underway.
Nowak pointed to the integration of Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System missiles on F-16s as a near-term solution, but said there is a hitch in getting those weapons in the field.

“It hasn’t happened yet, and we are trying to process it, but we [Polish Air Force] couldn’t get the fuses, which were utilized by the US Air Force, and were certified, because of business restrictions and limitations.
So we are waiting for the new type of the fuse,” he concluded.

Nowak also mentioned the possibility of using the F/A-50GF aircraft to combat drones, which Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced earlier this month has officially commenced combat duty.

items.title: 97% of US soldiers complete brain health assessment
items.originalTitle: 97% of US soldiers complete brain health assessment
items.summary: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release . The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making. evidenceRecords.text: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release .
The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making.
Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury.

Active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers in high-risk military occupational specialties, including combat engineers and explosive ordnance technicians, as well as troops operating heavy weapons systems, must take the assessment every year, starting soon after they enlist.
All other soldiers are required to test every three years.
Medical professionals use the data to monitor service members’ cognitive health throughout their military careers, allowing them to spot significant changes, including potential brain injuries.

“[The NCAT] is an important part of taking care of soldiers, but what this does is, it sets a baseline for reaction times and for memory,” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a release.

“By establishing a baseline for all soldiers, we’re able to monitor brain health, as well as … let medical providers help with treatment, if required.” According to the Sept. 30 release, the Army is expected to publish a directive about the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool and a broader overpressure program, which includes hazard assessment, exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, information management, illness and injury reporting and training and education.
“The takeaway is we are trying to take care of soldiers and monitor their health,” Gillis said.

“And if there is an impact, we’ll be able to treat them.” Reaching the milestone of 97% of soldiers being tested on the NCAT “demonstrates our commitment to cognitive safety, medical readiness and warfighting capability,” Gillis added.

The announcement of the milestone came just one month after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide the baseline cognitive assessments.

Artemis Security has launched Orion-1, an AI model that investigates and responds to cyberattacks on corporate networks on its own.

General-purpose AI models are becoming a growing problem for security teams, since the same skills also help attackers.
Artemis Security wants to close that gap with a purpose-built model.

US startup Artemis Security has launched Orion-1, a model designed to investigate and respond to attacks on corporate networks on its own, beating Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol on the company's own benchmark.

Orion-1 processes log data from auth services, cloud setups, corporate endpoints, SaaS apps, and network gear, then connects individual signals like a corporate account login, new cloud permissions, and a freshly created email inbox rule to tie them back to a single attacker.

Artemis fine-tuned Orion-1 on tasks drawn from its own security operations, including spotting suspicious patterns in log data, hunting for known attack techniques, writing new detection rules, and containing live attacks.
Artemis calls Orion-1 a "Frontier Foundation Model" but only describes this fine-tuning in its blog post, and it's unclear whether the company built on top of an existing model from another provider.
Artemis reports results across five tasks and tested Grok 4.7 and Kimi K3 alongside Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol.
The biggest gap shows up in attack reconstruction, where Orion-1 scored 80.8 compared to 58.3 for the next-best model.
Orion-1 is live in a private preview for select customers on the Artemis platform, where customers set limits per action type on how much the model can decide on its own.

items.title: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different
items.originalTitle: Flock CEO says its microphones detect ‘just gunshots’ — its website says different
items.summary: Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up. Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection, which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.

evidenceRecords.text: Flock CEO Garrett Langley said the company’s gunshot-detection microphones detect “just gunshots,” but Flock’s website paints a far broader picture of what other ambient audio also gets picked up.

Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt, the co-founder of the surveillance company defended Flock’s audio-collection product called Gunshot Detection, which listens for gunshots and other ambient audio across nearby neighborhoods to provide “earlier awareness” to potential public safety events.

Flock’s website says that the company’s audio systems can pinpoint gunfire instantly, while also being able to “detect street takeovers early to stop chaos before it escalates,” and “identify severe crashes in real time so help arrives faster.” It also says they can “expand awareness beyond gunfire with alerts for car crashes, fireworks, and sideshows.”
The company’s Gunshot Detection feature, announced last year, faced immediate pushback.

In announcing the feature, Flock said the technology would listen out for sounds of “screaming.” Privacy groups condemned the company for listening for human voices, prompting the company to amend its website to instead say “sounds of human distress.” Flock later said it pulled the ability to detect “distress” altogether from its customers who tried it.
When asked about the contradiction between his remarks and the company’s marketing materials that say the audio systems can detect more than gunshots, he responded, “It’s just gunshots.”

When reached by TechCrunch, Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel said: “Flock’s gunshot detection technology is primarily used to detect gunfire but is also capable of detecting fireworks, sideshows, and potential car crashes.

CEO Garrett Langley’s remarks were intended to emphasize that Flock’s Audio Detection technology is not designed to monitor conversations or analyze speech and does not currently detect human screaming or distress.”

An FAQ section of the website notes that “in addition to gunshots, Flock Gunshot and Audio Detection can detect fireworks, sideshows, and other disruptive community events.” It goes on to state that the company’s “detection library is continually expanding to include emerging threats that are relevant” to customers’ specific needs.

items.title: The Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone
items.originalTitle: The Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone
items.summary: After five-and-a-half years on Mars, NASA's Perseverance Rover has set a distance record for travel on another world. Since landing in Mars' Jezero Crater, an ancient paleolake, on February 18, 2021, Perseverance has travelled 45.22 km, or 28.10 miles. That puts it slightly ahead of NASA's Opportunity rover, which travelled 45.16 kilometers (28.06 miles) during its mission. It must be noted, however, that Perseverance took only 5.5 years to travel this far, while Opportunity required almost 15 years. Comparing the plutonium-powered Perseverance to the solar-powered Opportunity is unfair.

evidenceRecords.text: NASA's Perseverance Rover has reached another milestone.
After five-and-a-half years on Mars, NASA's Perseverance Rover has set a distance record for travel on another world.
Since landing in Mars' Jezero Crater, an ancient paleolake, on February 18, 2021, Perseverance has travelled 45.22 km, or 28.10 miles.
That puts it slightly ahead of NASA's Opportunity rover, which travelled 45.16 kilometers (28.06 miles) during its mission.
It must be noted, however, that Perseverance took only 5.5 years to travel this far, while Opportunity required almost 15 years.
Comparing the plutonium-powered Perseverance to the solar-powered Opportunity is unfair.
But in any case, Perseverance deserves recognition for this milestone.
“The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving.
We’ve blown well past that..." - Steven Lee, Perseverance and Curiosity project manager, JPL/NASA.
Perseverance is currently in a region named “Lac de Charmes,” which is off the western end of Jezero Crater.
It reached its new milestone while heading toward a feature named "Idubi," a scientific target notable for its ancient rocks.
On Earth, there are no rocks as old as these because they've all been destroyed by plate tectonics.
Perseverance has found igneous rocks, a surprising result considering that scientists expected to find mostly sedimentary rocks.
“The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path," said Mark Maimone, the deputy team chief of Perseverance's robotic operation.

items.title: Can AI understand space, time and pain?
items.originalTitle: Can AI understand space, time and pain?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence can do remarkable things, but how much does it actually understand about the world? Researchers have found that surprisingly specific information can be extracted from the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. Using mathematical tools to probe a model's internal activity, they can identify where a city is located on a map, when a historical figure lived or what emotion a character feels, even detecting descriptions of pain. Many have interpreted these findings as evidence that AI models build an internal picture of the world.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial intelligence can do remarkable things, but how much does it actually understand about the world?
Researchers have found that surprisingly specific information can be extracted from the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT.

Using mathematical tools to probe a model's internal activity, they can identify where a city is located on a map, when a historical figure lived or what emotion a character feels, even detecting descriptions of pain.
Many have interpreted these findings as evidence that AI models build an internal picture of the world.
Some have even linked them to debates about whether AI might have the capacity to suffer.
These questions have taken on new urgency as debate grows over whether AI systems could suffer or warrant moral consideration, prompting some companies to restrict harsh treatment of their chatbots.
But a new paper by Elan Barenholtz, Ph.D., of Florida Atlantic University suggests that the evidence may be weaker than it appears.
The paper, "World Properties Without World Models: Distributional Associations and the Interpretation of Decoding Results from Language Models," is available as a preprint on arXiv.
It examines whether the same information attributed to language models can be extracted from much simpler mathematical structures called word vectors.
These vectors capture patterns in which words tend to appear together, without accounting for context.
Barenholtz found that they can reveal much of the same information as LLMs.

"This suggests that being able to read something out of an AI system doesn't prove the system actually has a kind of internal model of those things," said Barenholtz, an associate professor of psychology in FAU's Charles E.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Quminex raised CAD $1.5 million in pre-seed financing to develop its mineral exploration technology, with Quantacet leading the round alongside QAI Ventures and angel investors.
The funding will support growth and development of the Quminex Discovery Platform, which uses machine learning to turn geological data into testable mineral exploration targets.
The investment was led by Quantacet, joined by QAI Ventures, and angel investors.
Quminex accelerates mineral exploration through advanced computational techniques.
By reducing geological uncertainty, the technology increases success rates and speeds up the discovery of critical mineral deposits.
Quminex transforms complex datasets into explainable and testable mineral system models using proprietary machine learning workflows, enabling smarter capital allocation.
Built on transparency, sustainability, and credibility, Quminex is committed to helping secure a stable, responsible supply of critical metals.
The financing will be used to accelerate growth and advance technological development of the Quminex Discovery Platform TM , an end-to-end exploration stack.
It is built on rigorous data preparation, feature engineering and feature selection tools, paired with powerful computational techniques and machine learning models.
“This $1.5 million pre-seed investment is a critical milestone, accelerating the development of the Quminex Discovery Platform,” said Marc Fassbender, CEO and Co-Founder of Quminex.
“By transforming early-stage exploration into a repeatable, data-driven process, we are changing how ore deposits can be discovered.

This capital will enable us to scale our proprietary platform to locate the critical mineral deposits essential for our society.” “Quminex is modernizing mineral exploration with a unique approach leveraging cutting-edge computing techniques.

displayTranslation.sourceSummary: Defence announcement comes after Jacqui Lambie tells parliament a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on board Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of a Royal Australian Navy ship in Cairns, the defence department has revealed, just hours after senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on the vessel.
